title: Reinforcement Learning
body:
An agent in an environment, learning what to do from consequences. No labelled examples, no
correct action supplied: only a number arriving after the fact, sometimes long after.

```
        ┌──────────── state sₜ, reward rₜ ────────────┐
        ↓                                             │
    ┌───────┐                                  ┌─────────────┐
    │ AGENT │ ───────── action aₜ ───────────→ │ ENVIRONMENT │
    └───────┘                                  └─────────────┘
```

The pieces: a **state** describing the situation, an **action** the agent may take, a **reward**
scoring what happened, and a **policy** $\pi(s)$ saying which action to take in which state.
Learning the policy is the entire task.

## Against the other two paradigms

| | Told | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| [[Supervised Learning]] | the right answer for each input | getting labels |
| [[Unsupervised Learning]] | nothing, only the data | no way to evaluate |
| **Reinforcement** | a number, later | **which action earned it** |

That last cell is the **credit assignment problem** and it is what makes RL its own field. Win a
chess game in 40 moves and the reward arrives once, at the end. Which of the 40 moves was good?
The reward does not say, and most of them were probably irrelevant.

The formal frame is a Markov decision process, defined by states, actions, transition
probabilities, and rewards. It has no note in the vault; what it adds beyond the picture above is
the Markov assumption, that the current state contains everything relevant and history can be
discarded. Same assumption a [[Finite State Machine]] makes.

## Return, discounting, and value

The agent maximises **return**, the total future reward, not the next one:

$$G_t = r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 r_{t+2} + \cdots$$

$\gamma \in [0, 1)$ is the **discount factor**, and it does two jobs: it keeps the sum finite on
tasks that never end, and it encodes how much the agent cares about the future. Low $\gamma$ is
short-sighted, high $\gamma$ is patient. The whole difference between an agent that grabs the
nearest reward and one that sets up a win two minutes later is that one number.

A **value function** $V(s)$ is the expected return from $s$, which is [[Expected Utility]] with
the utility unknown and being learned. That connection is the reason block 2 comes before block 5:
RL is decision theory where the probabilities and the utilities both have to be discovered.

## Passive and active

- **Passive**: the policy is fixed, and the agent is only learning how good it is (evaluating
  $V^\pi$). Simpler, and rarely what you want.
- **Active**: the agent chooses actions and improves the policy as it goes, which introduces the
  problem below.

## Exploration against exploitation

**Exploit** and take the best action you currently know, or **explore** and try something else to
find out whether your estimate is wrong? Pure exploitation locks in the first mediocre strategy
that works, because nothing ever tests the alternatives. Pure exploration learns everything and
uses none of it.

The standard fix is $\epsilon$-greedy: act greedily with probability $1 - \epsilon$, act randomly
otherwise, and decay $\epsilon$ over time. This is not a hack, it is the [[Expected Utility]]
value-of-information argument: exploring is rational because what you learn changes later
decisions.

## Rewards are the specification, and they are where it goes wrong

The reward function is the only thing telling the agent what you want, and it will be satisfied
exactly as written. Reward a vacuum for collecting dirt and it dumps dirt out to collect again;
reward a boat-racing agent for hitting checkpoints and it spins in circles hitting the same one
forever. **Reward shaping**, adding intermediate rewards to make learning faster, is where this
bites hardest, because a shaped reward the agent can farm becomes the whole behaviour.

Same failure as a badly written performance measure in [[Rational Agent]] and a badly written
fitness function in [[Genetic Algorithm]]. **Three blocks of this course, one mistake.** It is the
thing to remember from all of them.
